business: Night Shift: open-source app that runs a team's coding-agent pipelines overnight on their own computers and logins
by_segment: Tech lead at a small digital agency
Senior developer who picks the tools for a small team
Owner or managing director of a small agency who holds the budget
Founder or CTO of an early-stage startup
why_not: I already threw away most of the PRs background agents opened for us, and a pre-alpha tool from one developer doesn't change what the agent writes. Maybe I'd poke at the free self-hosted version on a slow Friday, but I'm not paying $99 a month for it.

The budget and loop guard speak directly to my fear, and the free self-hosted version on my spare Mac mini costs me nothing to try. But it is pre-alpha from one developer, so I would tinker with the free version before I pay $99 a month for anything.
We already get scheduled agent runs from Claude Code and GitHub as part of what we pay for. I would not add another tool and another bill for the same thing.

I already have a cron job calling claude -p and I'd rather add a budget check to it than adopt a pre-alpha tool from one developer. The budget and loop guard are the interesting part, but I can script those myself in an afternoon.

I'd self-host the free version before paying for Cloud, so the $99 isn't for me anyway. And my problem with background agents was never scheduling, it was PRs not worth reviewing, and nothing here says the output gets better.
flip: A clear demo where it reliably ships tested PRs overnight that our vendor scheduling cannot, plus some proof it will still exist in a year.

A few months of public use with proof the budget and loop limits actually stop runs, plus a way to import my existing scripts as a flow. Then I might self-host the free version.
A few weeks of the free version on my Mac mini that show the cost caps really stop runs, plus a second maintainer or a few agencies like mine using it.
Seeing it reliably beat my cron setup for a few weeks, with the approval step and cost caps actually saving us from bad overnight runs.
A few agencies like mine running it on real client work for a couple of months, with proof the budget stop actually held.
Proof from another agency that most overnight PRs actually got merged, plus a clear answer I can show clients about where their code goes.
A clear case where the vendor scheduling fails us, like budget overruns or runs looping overnight, plus a few named teams running it in production for months.

A few weeks on the free version where the budget caps actually hold and the morning PRs get merged without rework. After that I'd pay for the hosted server.
